title: Ship it responsibly: drift, fairness & the gate

steps.prompt: Your model hit 95% accuracy in the demo. Why might it be unsafe — and quietly getting worse — by next quarter?
steps.sub: Shipping an AI feature isn't a finish line, it's the start of a long tail you have to fund. By the end you'll spot model drift, catch the 95%-accurate-but-unfair trap, and run a responsible-AI ship gate before any AI feature goes live.

steps.prompt: The lifecycle doesn't end at deploy.
steps.sub: Tap each stage — note where most PMs stop, and where the real work lives.

cards.b: Gather data, train the model, measure it on a held-out set. This is the part everyone budgets for.
It goes live. Tempting to call it 'done' here — but the world is about to start changing underneath it.
Watch live accuracy, drift, and fairness in production. This costs money every month, not once.
When monitoring trips a trigger, gather fresh data and retrain. A PM must fund this loop, not just the first launch.

steps.prompt: A teammate says: 'The model passed eval at 95%, so we're done — ship and move on.' What's the PM-level correction?

options.t: Agree — a 95% eval score means the model is finished.
Deploy is the START of monitoring + retraining, which must be funded as an ongoing cost.
Re-run eval one more time to be safe, then never touch it again.

steps.why: Eval measures the model against yesterday's data. The moment it's live, the world starts drifting and accuracy decays. The lifecycle is data → train → eval → deploy → MONITOR → retrain — and monitor + retrain are a recurring line item a PM has to budget for, not a one-time launch task.
hints: What happens to the data the model sees AFTER it ships?
Which two stages come after 'deploy' — and how often do they run?

steps.prompt: Two ways a live model rots.
steps.sub: Tap each — these are the two flavors of model drift.

cards.b: The INPUTS change. New slang in support tickets, a younger user mix, a new product category. The questions coming in no longer look like the training data.
The input→output RELATIONSHIP changes. Fraudsters invent new tricks, so the same features now mean something different. The rules of the game moved.
Either way, the model that scored 95% in eval silently loses points in production — which is exactly why you monitor and retrain.

steps.prompt: Data drift or concept drift? Sort each scenario.
steps.sub: Tap a scenario, then a bin. Ask: did the INPUTS change, or the input→output RELATIONSHIP?

items.t: Gen-Z users flood your app and start using slang the model has never seen
Fraudsters discover a new scam pattern, so 'normal-looking' transactions are now fraud
A new region launches; incoming support questions are in a dialect not in training data
Post-pandemic, the same shopping signals that meant 'will buy' now mean 'just browsing'
Your camera supplier changes, so product photos suddenly have a warmer color tint
A new tax law changes what counts as a 'risky' loan, flipping the old approve/deny logic

hints: Data drift = the things coming IN look different. Concept drift = the same input now leads to a DIFFERENT correct answer.
If the world's rules moved (fraud, law, behavior shift), it's concept drift. If just the input distribution moved (new slang, new users, new tint), it's data drift.

steps.prompt: Inference vs training cost — true or false?
steps.sub: Tap each, then check together. This drives your unit economics.

statements.t: Training is mostly a one-time capital cost; inference is a per-request running cost that scales with usage.
statements.why: Right. You train once (big upfront bill), but every single user request costs you again at inference time — and for LLM products that running cost can dwarf training.

statements.t: A bigger model always improves quality with no downside.
statements.why: No — a bigger model usually means better quality BUT higher latency and higher per-request cost. It's a trade-off, not a free win.

statements.t: Caching, RAG, smaller models, and routing easy cases to a cheap model are all ways to control inference cost.
statements.why: Yes — these are the PM's levers: cache repeat answers, retrieve instead of using a huge model, pick a smaller model, or route simple requests to a cheap model and only hard ones to the expensive one.

hints: Which cost do you pay once, and which do you pay on every request?
Bigger model = better answers, but what happens to latency and cost per call?

steps.prompt: Your hiring-screen model is 95% accurate OVERALL. Legal asks if it's safe to ship. What's the right next question?
steps.sub: The aggregate number is hiding something. What do you check?

options.t: Nothing — 95% overall is high, ship it.
Check accuracy PER subgroup — a model can be 95% overall yet ~60% for a minority group the aggregate drowns out.
Just retrain on more data; accuracy will reach 99% and fairness takes care of itself.

steps.why: A high overall score is an average — and a small subgroup barely moves it. A model can be 95% overall and only ~60% for a minority subgroup, which in hiring, credit, or health is a real harm to real people. Always measure performance PER subgroup, not just in aggregate. More data alone doesn't guarantee fairness.
hints: An average can be high while a small slice is terrible. How do you see that slice?
Who gets hurt if the 5% of errors all land on one group?

steps.sub: Tap each check. Run ALL of these before shipping ANY AI feature.

cards.b: Measure performance for each subgroup, not just overall. Catch the 95%-but-60%-for-a-minority trap before users do.
Can you explain a decision to the level the domain needs? A loan denial or a medical flag needs a 'why' — a movie pick may not.
Minimal data, real consent, a deletion path, and PII protected. E.g. Acharya, our tutor, keeps only what it needs and lets a learner delete their data.
A dashboard watching live accuracy/drift, and a defined threshold that fires a retrain. Fund the long tail, don't hope.
An escalation path for high-stakes or low-confidence cases — Acharya hands a stuck learner to a human instead of guessing.
One accountable person for outcomes, plus a rollback plan. 'The algorithm did it' is not an acceptable answer.

steps.prompt: Which of these belong on the Responsible-AI ship gate? Tap ALL that apply.
steps.sub: Pick every check you'd require before shipping an AI feature.
chips: Explainability to the level the domain needs
Privacy: minimal data, consent, deletion path, PII protected
Drift monitoring with a retrain trigger
Human-in-the-loop / escalation for high-stakes or low-confidence cases
A named owner accountable for outcomes + a rollback plan
Highest possible overall accuracy is enough on its own
Ship fast and patch fairness later if someone complains
steps.why: The first six ARE the gate: per-subgroup accuracy, domain-appropriate explainability, privacy, drift monitoring + retrain trigger, a human escalation path, and a named owner with a rollback plan. The last two are the traps — a high overall number hides subgroup harm, and 'patch it later' means real people get hurt first. 'The algorithm did it' is never acceptable.
hints: Six of these you just tapped through on the gate cards.
Two chips describe shortcuts that skip accountability or hide subgroup harm — leave those out.

steps.prompt: Acharya (our AI tutor) gives a confident but WRONG answer on a high-stakes exam question. Which gate check would have caught this?
steps.sub: Map the failure to the missing check.

options.t: A bigger model — quality fixes everything.
A human-in-the-loop / escalation path for high-stakes or low-confidence cases.
More marketing so users expect occasional mistakes.

steps.why: High-stakes or low-confidence cases should route to a human instead of letting the model answer alone. An escalation path means a stuck or exam-critical learner gets a human, not a confident hallucination. Bigger models still make mistakes — the safeguard is the loop, not raw capability.
hints: Which gate check is specifically about high-stakes or low-confidence situations?
Who should the model hand off to when the cost of being wrong is high?

steps.sub: Not graded. Naming the weak spot in YOUR product is how this sticks.

fields.label: Which Responsible-AI gate check does your product most need right now — and why?
fields.ph: e.g. drift monitoring — our fraud model has no retrain trigger and rules keep changing

fields.label: What's one concrete step you'd take this month to close that gap?
fields.ph: e.g. add a per-subgroup accuracy dashboard before the next release

steps.prompt: Put the AI lifecycle in order — including the part that never ends.
steps.sub: Tap the stages in the right sequence.
chips: Monitor for drift + fairness in the wild
hints: Start with the raw material (data) and end with the loop that keeps it alive.
data → train → eval → deploy → monitor → retrain. Monitor and retrain are the long tail you fund.
